1219.title: bhakti: the Narada Bhakti Sutras complete
1219.hook: the last pages: what the people of this love are like, and the book's closing promise
1219.carry: bhakti: the Narada Bhakti Sutras complete
1219.howItsDone: In devotional Hindu communities, the closing sutras are read as a portrait of the ideal devotee, and the forms of love they list, such as servant, friend, parent and beloved, are familiar ways of relating to God in bhakti traditions.

segments.voice: Yesterday, bhakti as a taste that can't be told, like a taste for someone who cannot speak, growing every moment.

Two old friends meet after years apart and can't get a sentence out. One starts to speak and her voice catches. The other just laughs and wipes his eyes. Anyone watching knows exactly what's going on, though nobody has said a word. The last pages of the Narada Bhakti Sutras describe people like that, except the one they can't stop talking about is God. Today we finish the book.
screen: `OLD FRIENDS, NO WORDS.` → `VOICES CATCH.` → `THE LAST PAGES.`

segments.voice: The chief devotees, the sutras say, are those whose love has one direction only. When they talk with one another about the Lord, their throats choke, the hair on their arms stands up, and tears come. They purify their families and the earth. Then a startling line: they make the holy places holy, make actions good, and scriptures true. And among them there is no distinction of birth, learning, looks, family, wealth or work. Why? Because they are his. Tadiyah. Belonging to him outranks everything else on the list. Then some practical advice. Don't lean on argument: there's endless room for it, and it settles nothing. Read the books of love instead, and do what wakes it up. Don't waste even half a moment. Keep up the plain virtues: not harming, truthfulness, purity, compassion, faith. Near the end, the sutras say love, though one, takes eleven forms. Among them: love of his qualities and greatness, of his form, of worship, of remembering him; love as a servant, a friend, a parent, a beloved; giving oneself entirely, being wholly absorbed, and the deep ache of separation. Then a list of teachers who agree, fearless of what people say, among them Vyasa, Shandilya, Garga, Hanuman and Vibhishana. And the last line, said twice at its close: whoever trusts and has faith in this teaching of Narada becomes a devotee, and reaches the most beloved. So the book that opened with now, then, we will explain bhakti, ends with a promise. Tomorrow, the Alvar hymns: Tamil poet-saints who sang their love for Vishnu aloud.
screen: `THROATS CHOKE, TEARS COME.` · `THEY MAKE HOLY PLACES HOLY.` · `NO DISTINCTION: THEY ARE HIS.` · `ONE LOVE, ELEVEN FORMS.`

segments.voice: Let the sutras' forms of love drift past slowly: a servant's, glad to help; a friend's; a parent's, watching over; a beloved's; love that remembers; love that aches when apart. Don't choose; notice which one warms a little as it passes, toward God if you pray, or toward a person you love if not, and stay with that one.
Bhakti. In the last pages of the sutras, one love in eleven forms, and its people, among whom there is no distinction, because they are his.
Your line: bhakti: the Narada Bhakti Sutras complete. One love, many ways in. That's the book, finished.

1220.title: the Alvar hymns
1220.hook: a king's wish list: a fish in the temple pond, a tree on the hill, a step at the shrine's door
1220.howItsDone: In Sri Vaishnava worship, the Alvars' Tamil hymns are recited in temples and homes, and pilgrims at Tirupati are told of Kulasekhara Alvar's wish to be a step before the Lord.

segments.voice: Yesterday finished the Narada Bhakti Sutras: one love in eleven forms, and no distinction among its people, because they are his.

A king sits down to write a wish list. He already has the throne, the palace, the treasury, the army. So what does he wish for? To be a fish in a temple pond. A bird by the water. A flowering tree on a hill. And finally, a stone step at the door of a shrine, the kind people walk on without looking down. That king, in Sri Vaishnava tradition, is Kulasekhara, one of the Alvars, and the wish list is one of his hymns.
screen: `A KING'S WISH LIST.` → `A FISH, A BIRD, A TREE.` → `A STEP AT THE SHRINE'S DOOR.`

segments.voice: First, the Alvar hymns. The Alvars were poet-saints of Vishnu who sang in Tamil, and the tradition explains their name as people sunk deep in God. Their songs name real temples and real hills, and they speak as servants, lovers, mothers and friends. Year three met two of them, Andal and Nammalvar. Now Kulasekhara. Tradition remembers him as a king of the Chera country, on India's southwest coast, who loved the Lord more than his crown. His hymns are gathered as the Perumal Tirumozhi, the holy words of the king. In one set of verses he turns toward Venkatam, the sacred hill of Vishnu, and makes his wishes. Not to rule the earth, or even the heavens. To be something small on that hill: a bird by the pond, a fish in its water, a servant who carries things for the Lord, a tree that flowers there. And then the image that stayed. Let me lie as a step, he sings, so I can see your coral mouth. Stood on by everyone who comes, low and still, but always facing the Lord. The tradition says the threshold step of the shrine at Tirupati, on that hill, carries his name to this day: Kulasekharan padi, Kulasekhara's step. The verses end with something like: let me be anything at all on that hill. Notice what the king gives up. Not just wealth. Height. Everything in a royal life points upward, and his hymn points down, to the stone under people's feet, because from there you can see the one you love.
screen: `POET-SAINTS OF VISHNU, IN TAMIL.` · `KULASEKHARA, A KING WHO SANG.` · `LET ME LIE AS A STEP.` · `ANYTHING AT ALL ON THAT HILL.`

segments.voice: Let your gaze drop to the floor a little way in front of you, the height a step would see from, and let thoughts of rank, titles, who's ahead, what you're owed, pass over you like footsteps. Then lift your eyes just a little, toward a picture, a window or the open space ahead, and keep that one direction, the way the step keeps facing the shrine. If you pray, you can face God this way, from the threshold.
The Alvar hymns. Tamil songs to Vishnu by poet-saints the tradition calls sunk deep in God, like Kulasekhara, the king who asked to be a step.
Your line: the Alvar hymns. The lowest place can have the clearest view. I'll be here tomorrow.

1221.title: the Alvar hymns
1221.hook: a singer carried into the temple looks at the Lord from the feet up
1221.howItsDone: In Sri Vaishnava tradition, Tiruppan Alvar's Amalanadipiran is recited in daily worship, and devotees are taught to behold the deity in the temple from the feet upward.

segments.voice: Yesterday opened the Alvar hymns with Kulasekhara, the king who asked to be a step at the shrine's door, low and still, facing the Lord.

Feet first. In the old custom of greeting an elder by touching their feet, the hand reaches down before the eyes ever meet. One Alvar's hymn runs on that same instinct. Tradition says its singer, Tiruppan, came from a community of bards kept outside the temple at Srirangam, and sang to the Lord from the riverbank. And it says a priest, Lokasaranga, was told by the Lord himself to carry the singer inside on his own shoulders. He did.
screen: `FEET BEFORE FACE.` → `A SINGER KEPT OUTSIDE.` → `CARRIED IN ON A PRIEST'S SHOULDERS.`

segments.voice: The hymn is short, named by its opening words, Amalanadipiran: the spotless one, the first Lord. What's remarkable is its path. Tiruppan stands before the image of Vishnu reclining at Srirangam, and he doesn't take it all in at once. He looks the way a devotee bows, starting at the feet. The holy feet, he sings, have come into my eyes. Then his gaze rises, one verse at a time. The red cloth at the waist. The navel, from which the lotus grows that holds the creator Brahma. The chest, where the goddess Lakshmi dwells. The throat. The red mouth. The long, wide eyes. And then the whole dark, beautiful form at once. It's a slow, loving look, the kind you'd give a sleeping child. Each part reminds him of a story, too: the throat that once swallowed the worlds, the hand that holds the discus. Then the last verse turns, and it's the line people remember. Having seen my nectar, he says, these eyes of mine will not look at anything else. The tradition says that with this song he merged into the Lord. Whether you read that as a miracle or as a poem's way of saying everything was complete, the hymn itself is the point. Notice who sings it. A man kept outside the walls is carried in, and sings the hymn the temple keeps. Two days ago the Narada Bhakti Sutras said there is no distinction among those who love, because they are his. Here, on a priest's shoulders, is that line acted out.
screen: `AMALANADIPIRAN: THE SPOTLESS ONE.` · `THE GAZE BEGINS AT THE FEET.` · `RISING, PART BY PART, TO THE EYES.` · `THESE EYES WON'T LOOK ELSEWHERE.`

segments.voice: Choose something in front of you, an image you hold sacred if you have one, or a plant, or a face in a photo, and look only at the bottom of it for a breath or two. Then let the eyes rise a little at a time, staying with each part, and only at the top take it all in at once and rest there. If you pray, you can let this be a way of beholding God.
The Alvar hymns. In Tiruppan's Amalanadipiran, a gaze that rises from the Lord's feet to his eyes and then won't look at anything else.

1222.title: the Alvar hymns
1222.hook: a list of things a group of girls won't do for a month, and what they lean on when they finally reach Krishna's door
1222.howItsDone: In the month of Margazhi, Sri Vaishnava temples and households recite Andal's Tiruppavai before dawn, and teachers explain its verses on the rules of the vow and on the bond with the Lord that can't be undone.

segments.voice: Yesterday in the Alvar hymns, Tiruppan was carried into the temple and looked at the Lord from the feet up, one part at a time.
screen: `FROM THE FEET UP.` · `TODAY: THE RULES OF A VOW.`

segments.voice: No ghee. No milk. A bath before dawn. No kohl on the eyes, no flowers in the hair. That's part of a list, kept by the girls of Krishna's cowherd village as they set out on a vow for the month of Margazhi. The list is a hymn. Andal, one of the Alvars, sang it in her Tiruppavai, the song of the dawn vow. Year three walked with those girls as they woke each other in the dark and went knocking at Krishna's door. Today, two other pages of the same song: the rules they keep on the way, and what they say about themselves when they arrive.
screen: `NO GHEE. NO MILK.` → `NO KOHL, NO FLOWERS.` → `ANDAL'S TIRUPPAVAI.`

segments.voice: Early in the hymn, the girls set out the vow. They'll bathe before dawn. They'll go without ghee and milk. They won't line their eyes or put flowers in their hair. They won't do what shouldn't be done, and they won't go carrying harmful words about anyone. Then the list turns from giving up to giving: alms and gifts, as much as they're able. So the vow trims the comforts, guards the tongue, and opens the hand. At the end of the hymn, they finally stand before Krishna. You might expect them to list their merits: all those cold baths, all that missed ghee. They don't mention any of it. We follow the cows into the woods and eat there, they say. We're a cowherd clan with no learning at all. Our one good fortune is that you were born among us. Then the line Sri Vaishnava teachers keep coming back to: the bond between you and us can't be undone here, even if someone tried. We're children who don't know any better, they add; if, out of love, we called you by small names, don't be angry. A month of discipline, and at the door they don't hold it up. The vow got them out of bed in the dark. What they lean on is the bond: plain, a little sheepish, and completely sure of the relationship.

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you're close to, or God if you pray, and notice any urge to arrive with a list: what you've done for them, how hard you've tried, what you've given up. Let the list go quiet, one item at a time, and rest in the plain fact of the bond, with nothing to show. If a small, fond name for them comes to mind, let it come.
The Alvar hymns. Today, Andal's dawn vow: comforts trimmed, the tongue guarded, the hand open, and at the door, only the bond.

1223.title: the Alvar hymns
1223.hook: three strangers squeeze into one dark shelter in the rain, someone unseen presses in, and each lights a lamp with a song
1223.howItsDone: Sri Vaishnavas tell the story of the three Alvars at Tirukkovalur, and their three linked hymns are recited as part of the collection of Alvar songs in temples and homes.

segments.voice: Yesterday in the Alvar hymns, Andal's girls kept a vow of small renunciations, and at Krishna's door leaned only on the bond.
screen: `THE BOND AT THE DOOR.` · `TODAY: A LAMP IN THE DARK.`

segments.voice: Rain, hard and sudden, at night, in a town called Tirukkovalur. A wandering singer ducks into a tiny covered passage, room enough for one to lie down. A second soaked stranger asks to come in. Room for one to lie, the first says, means room for two to sit. A third arrives. Room for two to sit means room for three to stand. So three strangers stand shoulder to shoulder in the dark, dripping. Then the space gets tighter, as if a fourth body has pressed in among them. Nobody came through the door. That's the story the Sri Vaishnava tradition tells about how three of the Alvar hymns began.
screen: `RAIN, AND ROOM FOR ONE.` → `TWO SIT. THREE STAND.` → `A FOURTH PRESSES IN.`

segments.voice: The three, the story goes, were Poygai, Bhutam and Pey. Crammed in the dark with someone unseen, they don't panic or push. Each one lights a lamp, and the lamps are songs. Poygai sings a lamp on the scale of the world: the earth for the bowl, the ocean for the oil, the blazing sun for the flame, offered at the feet of the Lord. Bhutam answers with a lamp on the scale of a heart: love for the bowl, longing for the oil, a mind melting with joy for the wick, lit as a lamp of knowing. In that double light, Pey sings what he sees. The fourth one, pressing in, is Vishnu, with Lakshmi, the goddess of fortune, beside him. I have seen, he sings, and he names it: the goddess, a golden form, a color like the blazing sun, the wheel, the conch. A lamp as big as the cosmos, a lamp as close as feeling, then sight. The tradition doesn't ask you to choose between the huge and the intimate; it lights both, and God turns out to have been standing among them the whole time. Each Alvar's verses became a hymn of its own, sung in a linked form called antadi: the last word of one verse becomes the first of the next, like hands passing a flame.
screen: `THREE ALVARS, ONE DARK SHELTER.` · `A LAMP AS BIG AS THE WORLD.` · `A LAMP MADE OF LOVE.` · `I HAVE SEEN.`

segments.voice: Light two lamps. First the wide one: let your attention open to everything at once, the floor holding you, the air, the sky above the roof. Then the close one: bring to mind someone or something you love, and let that warmth fill the chest like oil in a small bowl. Sit in both kinds of light and see who seems near; if you pray, let the one you pray to be the one who's near.
The Alvar hymns. Today, three singers in one dark shelter, two lamps, and a fourth who was already there.
Your line: the Alvar hymns. They made room in the dark, and someone was already there. Go gently.

1224.title: the Alvar hymns
1224.hook: God appears in the sky over a city, and the old devotee's first worry is that someone might put the evil eye on him
1224.howItsDone: Sri Vaishnavas sing Periyalvar's Tiruppallandu in their temples and homes as a blessing over the Lord, alongside Periyalvar's songs of Yashoda and the child Krishna.

segments.voice: Yesterday in the Alvar hymns, three strangers in the rain lit a lamp as big as the world and a lamp made of love, and found Vishnu standing among them.
screen: `TWO LAMPS IN THE DARK.` · `TODAY: A BLESSING FOR GOD.`

segments.voice: A grandmother sees a beautiful baby in the street and, before anything else, says a quick word against the evil eye. Too much praise, the old worry goes, and something bad might follow. Now move that instinct. The Sri Vaishnava tradition tells of a temple garland-maker named Vishnuchitta who, on a day of great honor, looked up and saw Vishnu himself in the sky, riding the eagle Garuda, come to watch. Crowds everywhere. The old man's first feeling wasn't awe, or a request. It was worry: someone might cast the evil eye on him. So he did what that grandmother does. He sang a blessing over God.
screen: `A WORD AGAINST THE EVIL EYE.` → `VISHNU IN THE SKY.` → `THE OLD MAN WORRIES FOR HIM.`

segments.voice: The blessing is the Tiruppallandu, and its key word is pallandu, many years. Many years, many years, the song begins, to your holy feet. Then the blessing spreads: many years to the goddess at your side, to the wheel and to the conch. It's what you sing over a child or an elder you love, and here it's sung to the Lord of the universe. Tradition says that's why Vishnuchitta came to be called Periyalvar, the great Alvar. Tradition says he also found and raised Andal, whose dawn vow came two days ago, so a father and a daughter both sit among the Alvars. His longer hymns keep the same tenderness. In them he sings as Yashoda, Krishna's foster mother: rocking the cradle, coaxing the toddler to come for his bath, calling the moon down to play with him. God as a little one who needs looking after. Hindu teachers have a word for this kind of love: vatsalya, a parent's love, given back to God. A prayer can bring God a need. Periyalvar brings God his care. Love, in these hymns, isn't only receiving protection; it's wanting to protect. A small worry from a big heart, and Sri Vaishnavas still sing it.
screen: `PALLANDU: MANY YEARS.` · `A BLESSING SUNG OVER GOD.` · `SINGING AS YASHODA.` · `LOVE THAT WANTS TO PROTECT.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you love and see them clearly, their face, their hands. Instead of wanting anything from them, wish them long life, many years, many years, letting the wish travel out with each breath. If another person comes to mind, bless them too; if you pray, let the blessing rise toward the name you pray to, the way Periyalvar did.
The Alvar hymns. Today, Periyalvar's many years: a blessing sung over God, and the love of a parent given back to the divine.
Your line: the Alvar hymns. Many years, sung over the one who keeps the world. That's today, done.

1225.title: the Alvar hymns
1225.hook: pilgrims sing ten verses that say they're part of a thousand, and a teacher sets out to find the rest
1225.howItsDone: Sri Vaishnavas chant Nammalvar's Tiruvaymoli in temples and homes alongside the Sanskrit Veda, and remember Nathamuni as the teacher who recovered the hymns.

segments.voice: Yesterday in the Alvar hymns, Periyalvar looked up at God and sang a blessing over him: many years.
screen: `MANY YEARS.` · `TODAY: TEN VERSES, AND A THOUSAND.`

segments.voice: Ten verses, sung by pilgrims at the temple in Kumbakonam. A teacher named Nathamuni hears them and is moved. Then he hears the last verse say these ten are part of a thousand. A thousand? He asks the pilgrims for the rest. They don't have them. He asks everywhere. Nobody does. That, the Sri Vaishnava tradition says, is how a lost Tamil scripture began to come home. Year three met its singer, Nammalvar, the silent boy under the tamarind who answered a riddle. Today, how his songs were nearly lost, and found.
screen: `TEN VERSES AT KUMBAKONAM.` → `TEN OUT OF A THOUSAND?` → `NOBODY HAS THE REST.`

segments.voice: So Nathamuni goes to Tirukkurugur, Nammalvar's town, to the tamarind where the silent boy once sat. Nobody there has the thousand either. But, tradition says, someone gives him a short hymn: the one Madhurakavi, Nammalvar's disciple, sang in praise of his teacher. Recite this, he's told. He does, over and over, until Nammalvar appears to him and gives back the hymns. Nathamuni sets them to music and teaches them, and his line of teachers would later reach Ramanuja. Notice the key that opened the door: not a library, not a clever search, but a disciple's song of love for his teacher. What came back is the Tiruvaymoli, longing set to verse. Sometimes Nammalvar sings as himself. Sometimes he sings as a girl missing her beloved, sending birds as messengers to Vishnu. And sometimes the joy is so full that God and the singer seem to have swallowed each other. Tradition calls this song the Tamil Veda, and Sri Vaishnavas speak of two Vedantas, one in Sanskrit and one in Tamil, read together.
screen: `TO THE TAMARIND AT TIRUKKURUGUR.` · `A DISCIPLE'S SHORT HYMN.` · `THE SONGS GIVEN BACK.` · `THE TAMIL VEDA.`

segments.voice: Walk back through the Alvar days, one breath for each: the king who asked to be a step, Tiruppan's slow look from the feet up, Andal's girls at the door, three lamps in the rain, Periyalvar's many years, and ten verses that led to a thousand. Don't weigh them; notice which one stays a moment longer, and rest there. If you pray, you can offer that moment to God.
The Alvar hymns. Today, Nammalvar's Tiruvaymoli, lost and found again through a disciple's small hymn, which the tradition calls the Tamil Veda.
Your line: the Alvar hymns. Ten verses, one small hymn sung again and again, and a thousand came home. Until tomorrow.
